newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans pundits wonder if Kohl tired of office.
newsitem.headline: Germans pundits wonder if Kohl tired of office.

text.p: Germany's political rumour mill shifted into high gear on Thursday after Helmut Kohl's loyal crown prince, Wolfgang Schaeuble, dropped a heavy hint that he would like to become chancellor one day.

Newspaper commentators speculated whether Kohl might not run for re-election in 1998 or even step aside in frustration at growing unemployment to make way for a grand coalition under Schaeuble with the opposition Social Democrats.

Schaeuble, 54, the powerful parliamentary leader for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), ended years of discretion about the succession issue by telling Stern magazine the chancellor's job was a temptation he could probably not resist.

While underlining his loyalty and predicting the veteran chancellor would run again next year, Schaeuble bluntly said he felt fit for the job despite the fact he was paralysed from the chest down by a would-be assassin's bullet in 1990.
"Schaeuble has thrown his hat into the ring," said Essen's Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung. "This is the first time a CDU politician speaks of himself as a successor to Kohl."
The Stuttgarter Zeitung said: "A pro like Wolfgang Schaeuble weighs his words. So it's clear -- the crown prince is staking his claim, more openly and clearly than ever."
Kohl, 66, who last October became Germany's longest-serving post-war chancellor, has resolutely refused to say whether he will run again in the federal election due in late 1998.

Pundits unanimously agreed that Schaeuble, who served Kohl as chancellery and interior minister before taking over the crucial parliamentary post only a year after being confined to a wheelchair, would not stage a palace coup.
Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote that the succession issue could not have been brought up "without at least Kohl's quiet consent."

"This may have resulted from all the political monkey business in Bonn recently, which has already soured things for Kohl in the past," the paper wrote, referring to the political trench warfare within the centre-right coalition over cutting taxes and trimming budgets to qualify for Europe's single currency.

RTL Television recalled the CDU's problems with its liberal Free Democratic coalition partners, who have tested Kohl's party by pushing hard for tax cuts without saying how the resulting revenue shortfalls would be financed.
"The CDU's dissatisfaction with the FDP is slowly growing and the mood could swing towards support for a grand coalition," it commented.

Bonn has seen only one CDU-SPD national government, which was formed to win broad support to fight a recession in 1966, and politicians see such "grand coalitions" as a last chance option to deal with major challenges.

"Kohl would not be ready to be chancellor of a grand coalition with the SPD," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote. "That would be Schaeuble's hour, and it could come quickly with these rising unemployment rates and worsening financial problems."
The Stuttgarter Zeitung also speculated that foreign policy could be a factor in the timing of Schaeuble's remarks.

The European Union's Amsterdam summit in June and the July NATO summit in Madrid could set the EU firmly on the way to its planned single currency and open the Atlantic Alliance to new members from eastern Europe -- two key goals for Kohl.
"The attraction for him will fade if the unification of the old continent is irreversable and the relationship with Russia has been settled at the same time," it wrote.
"From the middle of 1997, everything is possible -- including the chance that Wolfgang Schaeuble's star rises."

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung took a more distanced view of the speculation about Schaeuble's comments: "Some people will certainly hear in them a groan under the drudgery of being so loyal to Kohl. But maybe it is only the air escaping from a trial balloon."
